topic: Mirror reflection and upright/inverted shadow intervals
problem: Sunrays are reflected from a horizontal mirror and fall on a vertical screen. An oblong object is placed on the mirror (Fig. 237). Describe the shadow on the screen.
solution: The supplied solution introduces an object height, an object-screen distance and an incidence angle. For a sufficiently distant screen, with l ≥ h tan α, a direct (upright) and an inverted shadow have adjoining bases and a total length 2h. For l < h tan α the total shadow is shorter than 2h and part of the screen is illuminated by neither direct nor reflected rays.
solution_note: Summary of the supplied solution substance, not a claim of verbatim transcription. The supplied solution calls the two far-screen portions a “direct” (upright) and an inverted shadow. In the formal model upright/inverted describe two orientations of reflected-light loss, while directBlocked is reserved for actual blockage of the unreflected sunlight channel. This distinction is an audit result obtained by solving the actual ray geometry; source terminology does not automatically determine formal physical-channel terminology.
diagram_caption:
Fig. 237 shows a two-dimensional vertical cross-section.

A horizontal mirror lies along the bottom.
A vertical screen stands on the mirror to the right.
An upright oblong object stands on the mirror between the incoming rays and the screen.
The object is represented in the cross-section as a vertical segment with its lower endpoint on the mirror.
Sunrays are represented by mutually parallel straight rays incident obliquely downward toward the horizontal mirror.
The rays are reflected from the horizontal mirror and the reflected rays propagate toward the vertical screen.
The object lies horizontally between at least some incident/reflected ray paths and the screen.

formal_interpretation: Use mirror y=0, opaque segment x=0 with height h>0, screen x=l>0, and acute incidence α measured from the vertical normal to the horizontal mirror. Ideal parallel straight rays, an extended mirror/screen and the reusable PhyslibTemp ideal specular reflection law form the model. Derive actual boundary-ray intersections, upright and inverted reflected-channel deficit intervals and the transition at l=h tan α. Classify direct/reflected illumination separately from orientation. Prove far union length 2h, and near union length h+l/tan α<2h with fully dark interval [0,h-l/tan α]. The explicit near formulas are derived strengthenings, not quoted source text.
